title: The Return of the Son of Man

verses.text: As Jesus was leaving the temple, one of His disciples said to Him, "Teacher, look at the magnificent stones and buildings!"
"Do you see all these great buildings?" Jesus replied. "Not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down."
While Jesus was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked Him privately,
"Tell us, when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to be fulfilled?"
Jesus began by telling them, "See to it that no one deceives you.
Many will come in My name, claiming, 'I am He,' and will deceive many.
When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come.
Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places, as well as famines. These are the beginning of birth pains.
So be on your guard. You will be delivered over to the councils and beaten in the synagogues. On My account you will stand before governors and kings as witnesses to them.
And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations.
But when they arrest you and hand you over, do not worry beforehand what to say. Instead, speak whatever you are given at that time, for it will not be you speaking, but the Holy Spirit.
Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child. Children will rise against their parents and have them put to death.
You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.
So when you see the abomination of desolation standing where it should not be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.
Let no one on the housetop go back inside to retrieve anything from his house.
And let no one in the field return for his cloak.
How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers!
Pray that this will not occur in the winter.
For those will be days of tribulation unseen from the beginning of God's creation until now, and never to be seen again.
If the Lord had not cut short those days, nobody would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom He has chosen, He has cut them short.
At that time if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'There He is!' do not believe it.
For false Christs and false prophets will appear and perform signs and wonders to deceive even the elect, if that were possible.
So be on your guard; I have told you everything in advance.
But in those days, after that tribulation: 'The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light;
the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.'
At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory.
And He will send out the angels to gather His elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.
Now learn this lesson from the fig tree: As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near.
So also, when you see these things happening, know that He is near, right at the door.
Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.
No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
Be on your guard and stay alert! For you do not know when the appointed time will come.
It is like a man going on a journey who left his house, put each servant in charge of his own task, and instructed the doorkeeper to keep watch.
Therefore keep watch, because you do not know when the master of the house will return—whether in the evening, at midnight, when the rooster crows, or in the morning.
Otherwise, he may arrive without notice and find you sleeping.
And what I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!"

context.author: Traditionally John Mark, a companion of Peter
context.genre: Apocalyptic discourse — Jesus' longest single teaching block in Mark, delivered privately to His four closest disciples on a mountainside overlooking the very temple He has just left
context.audience: Roman Christian readers, quite possibly already living through the persecution and upheaval this chapter describes, needing both warning and hope
context.setting: Seated on the Mount of Olives directly across the Kidron Valley from the temple, Jesus can see the very buildings He has just predicted will be leveled — a detail that gives His words unusual visual weight for the four disciples listening.
context.custom: Fleeing to rooftops or leaving a field in progress reflects real first-century Judean village life, where houses had external staircases to flat roofs and fields lay just outside town — Jesus' warnings assume His listeners' actual physical surroundings.
context.timelineImmediate: This is Jesus' last extended teaching before the Passion narrative begins in chapter 14 — a private discourse answering the disciples' question about the temple's coming destruction that widens into a broader picture of the era between His first and second coming.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' description of the Son of Man "coming in the clouds with great power and glory" directly quotes Daniel 7:13-14's vision of an exalted figure given everlasting dominion, while the darkened sun and falling stars echo Isaiah 13:10 and Joel 2:10's earlier prophetic imagery for divine judgment.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus predicts the temple's total destruction, then privately tells Peter, James, John, and Andrew what to watch for — wars, earthquakes, false messiahs, and a specific "abomination of desolation" that should trigger immediate flight. He closes by admitting even He doesn't know the exact day or hour, only the Father does, and presses the same point four different ways: stay awake, keep watch.

translation.meaning: The pains of labor and childbirth — used to describe early, escalating signs that point toward something inevitable, not yet the culmination itself.

occurrences.note: Also used once, strikingly, for "the pains of death" that could not hold Jesus in the tomb (Acts 2:24).

translation.meaning: The same word that opens the whole book in Mark 1:1 — here Jesus ties its worldwide proclamation directly to the timeline of the end.

translation.greek: τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως (to bdelygma tēs erēmōseōs)
translation.meaning: A detestable act that causes desecration — directly quoting the phrase from the book of Daniel, which Jesus tells His hearers to "understand" by returning to that text themselves.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's fuller parallel account of this same Olivet Discourse.
Luke's version, which adds explicit mention of Jerusalem being "surrounded by armies."

otBackground.note: The three passages behind Jesus' phrase "abomination of desolation," which He tells His hearers to go read themselves.
Earlier prophetic images of cosmic upheaval — darkened sun, falling stars — echoed directly in v.24-25.
The Son of Man receiving everlasting dominion and glory — directly quoted in Jesus' description of His own return.

commentary.note: Henry notices the disciples trying to draw Jesus back into admiring the temple He'd just left in disgust — "how apt many of Christ's own disciples are to idolize things that look great." His response, Henry notes, shows "how little Christ values external pomp, where there is not real purity": impressive architecture offers no protection when what it houses has gone rotten.

Ancient historians record that when Roman forces under Titus burned the temple in AD 70, gold decoration melted and ran into the cracks between the stones — leading soldiers to pry apart literally every stone in the search for it. Whatever the original intent behind Jesus' words, "not one stone left upon another" was fulfilled with striking, almost accidental literalness.

Gill notes a small geographical detail: the disciples sat with Jesus 'over against the temple' on the Mount of Olives specifically because the temple's eastern wall was lower than the rest, giving them a genuinely full, unobstructed view of the massive Herodian structure they were admiring.
